title: Box-bound bag
summary: Two flat panels, a gusset ring wrapping their perimeter, a zipper panel forming one face of that ring, and binding wrapping every raw edge. The binding is the seam: the two pieces meet wrong sides together with their allowances pointing outward, and one line of stitching catches binding, sandwich and binding in a single pass. Nothing here depends on the size — only on the materials and the machine, which is why one file serves every bag in the family.

sources.title: Mechanical Predictors of Discomfort during Load Carriage
sources.gives: static peak pressure predicts 85–86% of discomfort; 16 kPa blood-occlusion threshold; the hip tolerates 2.14× the shoulder's pressure for equal discomfort

sources.title: The Influence of Backpack Weight and Hip Belt Tension on Movement and Loading in the Pelvis and Lower Limbs during Walking
sources.gives: hip belt tension magnitude had no significant effect on gait — so cinch for stability, not for load transfer

sources.title: The 14 Best Fanny Packs — GearJunkie / OutdoorGearLab testing
sources.gives: 1–3 L capacity band; narrow webbing straps called out as uncomfortable; buckle landing on the hip named as a specific complaint; unpadded packs still rated comfortable

sources.title: Zipper Direction in Bag Making
sources.gives: a belt bag's zip should open away from the body's centre toward the dominant hand

sources.title: Conical hipbelt shape — Backpacking Light
sources.gives: the top and bottom arcs of a hip belt are not concentric, because the body under it is a truncated cone

sources.title: Backpack back system guide — foam and spacer mesh
sources.gives: 4–6 mm EVA is the usual back-panel padding; 6–10 mm for belts; 3D spacer mesh comes 3 mm or 6 mm

docs.title: A zipped pocket built into a panel

assembly.title: Test on scrap before you cut anything
assembly.stitch: straight, 3.0–3.5 mm, walking foot
assembly.body: Sew a bound seam on offcuts and measure the seam allowance you actually achieve. Every dimension in this pattern keys off {sa}, and a binding run that drifts to 5/16" makes the ring {ring} too short for the panels it has to wrap. Then sew the worst stack in the thickness table. If the machine will not drive it, change the tabs to doubled shell fabric now rather than after the fabric is cut.

figures.caption: What you are testing: the whole stack in one line of stitching. If the machine will not drive this on scrap it will not drive it on the bag.

assembly.title: Pre-wash and dry the shell
assembly.body: The shell is a natural fibre and it shrinks. This bag has no ease anywhere to absorb that, so a first wash after assembly distorts it. Wash and dry before cutting, and press.

assembly.title: Cut, and leave the gusset long
assembly.body: Rotary-cut everything, against a metal straightedge. The shell is synthetic and does not ravel, so no edge needs turning under and a hot knife is OPTIONAL rather than required — it will seal this cloth, but on a coated face it can leave a hard bead, so test on a scrap first. Raw edges DO survive to the finished bag and they are fine: every lap join shows one, clamped under two rows of topstitching within {lap}, and the placket's free edge hangs loose. Seal the placket's edge with a lighter if you like — it is the only one nothing holds. Leave the lap edges alone: a hot knife can leave a hard bead on a coated face, and a bead down the middle of a lap is a ridge the foot has to climb. Clips only, never pins — a pin hole in a coated shell is permanent and it is a hole in the waterproofing. If the cloth has a right side, cut EVERY piece with it facing the same way, binding strips included: a single-fold binding shows on both faces of the bag, so a strip cut face-down puts the wrong side outward and it will not match the strip next to it. Cut the gusset at {gusset_cut_long} rather than its finished {gusset_cut} and leave it long until the ring is fitted — the ring's true length depends on the allowance you actually achieve and on how hard the binding pulls, which is why good patterns give more than the calculation and let you trim. Any piece that carries embroidery is cut OVERSIZED and trimmed to size after the machine is done with it — see the next step. Where the pattern rounds a corner, cut the panels round a template rather than by eye — the two panels and the outer lower pieces all share that radius, and a corner that disagrees with its neighbour shows up as a pucker in the binding.

figures.caption: The gusset is cut LONG and trimmed later. Nothing is joined yet — this is the offcut you will lose once the ring has been fitted.

assembly.title: Cut, and leave the gusset long
assembly.body: Rotary-cut anything that does not melt-seal; hot-knife webbing and synthetic binding tape. Clips only, never pins. Cut the gusset at {gusset_cut_long} rather than its finished {gusset_cut} and leave it long until the ring is fitted — the ring's true length depends on the allowance you actually achieve and on how hard the binding pulls, which is why good patterns give more than the calculation and let you trim. Where the pattern rounds a corner, cut the panels round a template rather than by eye — the two panels and the outer lower pieces all share that radius, and a corner that disagrees with its neighbour shows up as a pucker in the binding.

figures.caption: The gusset is cut LONG and trimmed later. Nothing is joined yet — this is the offcut you will lose once the ring has been fitted.

assembly.title: Fold under every raw edge that will show
assembly.body: The shell frays, so the four edges that would otherwise be sealed each need ¼" pressed under: the zip strip laps where they lie on the tape, any rib or pocket long edges, pocket tops, and the overlapping end of each gusset lap join. Add that ¼" to the cut before you cut, not after. A narrow zigzag along each raw edge is faster and uglier, and fine on the ones that end up inside.

assembly.title: Embroider now, flat, before anything is assembled
assembly.body:
Any panel that carries a logo has to be stitched flat, before webbing or a pocket is behind it. Design to 96 mm or less — this machine's field is 100 × 100 mm.

THE PIECE IS USUALLY TOO SMALL TO HOOP: the frame's window is 100 mm and it needs fabric well past that on every side to clamp, so a 4⅛" outer pocket piece or a 2⅞" gusset cannot go in one at all. AND ON A COATED OR WATERPROOF SHELL IT MUST NOT BE HOOPED EVEN IF IT FITS — the ring compresses the coating and the mark can be permanent, and the standard cure for hoop burn is a low iron, which destroys the coating instead. Both problems have the same answer: embroider an OVERSIZED BLANK and cut the piece out of it afterwards, floating the blank on sticky-back tear-away that is hooped by itself — score the paper inside the ring, peel it, press the blank down, and BASTE it. Never pin: a pin hole in a coated cloth is permanent and it is outside the design where nothing will cover it. The Operation Manual describes the float on p.64.

Read `docs/05-materials-and-consumables.md` before the first one — on a coated shell the needle is a 75/11 SHARP rather than the heavier needle the seams want, every hole is a hole in the waterproofing, and the design wants to be open rather than solid for the same reason. On dark shell fabric read `docs/14-designing-for-dark-cloth.md` in full and declare the cloth, or it comes off speckled. On a narrow strap read `docs/16-narrow-material.md`. Use a stabilizer you can baste rather than iron: a coated or waxed shell will not take a fusible, and heat is the one thing most waterproof finishes cannot survive.

figures.caption: Every face that carries a design, and each is a separate hooping. After this step none of them can be stitched flat again.

assembly.title: Chassis webbing onto the gusset INTERIOR
assembly.stitch: straight, both long edges, 3.0 mm, walking foot
assembly.body: Mark the centreline on the gusset's inside face. Lay the {loop} length of {web} webbing along it so {gusset_face} sits on the gusset with equal tails free at each end, and topstitch both long edges. Raise the upper tension for this pass — thick webbing pulls the top thread down and leaves loops underneath at normal tension. Nothing threads onto the webbing; rings live on external tabs and tack through to it.

figures.caption: The tack itself, in the order it is sewn — one edge gets retraced, which is correct. Every box-X on this bag is thick enough to want hand-wheeling.

assembly.title: Pockets onto the gusset, over the webbing
assembly.stitch: straight, 3.5 mm, walking or Teflon foot
assembly.body: Bind each pocket's top edge first, then topstitch the other three edges down. Hold them with double-sided basting tape rather than clips — a pocket that shifts a sixteenth shows, and you cannot pin a coated panel. The pockets sit over the webbing and their own stitching helps hold it flat.

assembly.title: Build the zipper panel
assembly.stitch: straight, two rows, 3.0 mm, zipper foot, Microtex 90/14
assembly.body: Lap the {strip_front} strip and the {strip_rear} strip {lap} onto the zipper tape and topstitch two rows on each. Done right the coil ends up {coil_c} from the panel's cut edge — deliberately OFF-CENTRE, so the face centreline stays clear for the webbing. Basting tape holds the lap while you sew. The panel is cut {zip_cut} long — {zip_face} of opening plus {lap} at each end for the gusset to lap over, and it is the ONLY piece that carries that allowance. The finished panel measures {gusset_w} across, to match the gusset.

figures.caption: The panel this bag needs, at its own strip widths — and the finished width it has to match.
The same join in section: nothing is cut open, the zipper BECOMES a strip of the panel.

assembly.title: Build the zipper panel
assembly.stitch: straight, two rows, 3.0 mm, zipper foot, Microtex 90/14
assembly.body: Lap the {strip_front} strip and the {strip_rear} strip {lap} onto the zipper tape and topstitch two rows on each. The two strips are the same width here and the coil lands {coil_c} from the panel's cut edge, dead CENTRE — there is no chassis, so there is no webbing to keep the centreline clear for. That is what let this bag's belt width be decided on comfort rather than on clearance. Basting tape holds the lap while you sew. The panel is cut {zip_cut} long — {zip_face} of opening plus {lap} at each end for the gusset to lap over, and it is the ONLY piece that carries that allowance. The finished panel measures {gusset_w} across, to match the gusset.

figures.caption: The panel this bag needs, at its own strip widths — and the finished width it has to match.
The same join in section: nothing is cut open, the zipper BECOMES a strip of the panel.

assembly.title: Lay the chain the right way up
assembly.body:
**Reverse coil**, so the OUTSIDE of the bag shows flat tape and the spiral is underneath. Lay the chain **coil-DOWN** on the bench and lap the shell onto the tape from above.

Check it before the first row, because there is no undo: close the zip, put it on the bench the way the bag will hang, and look at it. If you can see the spiral, turn it over. Get this wrong and the finished bag has its pull on the INSIDE with both laps already sewn, and unpicking them means re-cutting the strips — the needle holes stay.

A reverse slider is a different part from a standard one. Check the slider against the chain before you build anything round it.

figures.caption: The two make-ups compared. Whichever you have, the rule is the same: the face you will SEE goes up, because the slider and its pull have to end up on that side.

assembly.title: Lay the chain the right way up
assembly.body:
**Standard coil**, so the spiral is meant to be seen. Lay the chain **coil-UP**, facing you, and lap the shell onto the tape either side of it. This is the conventional way round and the simpler of the two — there is no hidden face to get backwards.

Check it anyway before the first row, because there is no undo: close the zip, put it on the bench the way the bag will hang, and look at it. You should see the spiral and the pull. If you are looking at flat tape, turn it over — the finished bag would have its pull on the INSIDE with both laps already sewn, and unpicking them means re-cutting the strips.

Two things follow from standard coil, neither of them a problem. The closed opening reads as a ZIP rather than as a seam, so on the back pocket the placket is doing all of the hiding rather than half of it — set it carefully. And an upward-facing spiral collects grit and holds water where a reverse one sheds; on a waterproof shell the main top zip is then the wettest line on the bag, so if it will live outdoors, park it under the flap of whatever it sits beside and keep it closed.

figures.caption: The two make-ups compared. Whichever you have, the rule is the same: the face you will SEE goes up, because the slider and its pull have to end up on that side.

assembly.title: Shorten the zipper and make a new stop
assembly.stitch: dense zigzag ~3 mm wide at 0.4 mm, 5–6 passes
assembly.body: Open it halfway, then bar-tack across the coil at the new length: this machine has no programmed bar-tack, so work a dense zigzag back and forth. Trim 1" beyond it and cap each cut end with a scrap. A coil zipper cut without a new stop lets the slider run straight off the end, and there is no putting it back on.

figures.caption: Tack first, trim 1" beyond it, then cap. Flush leaves the tack at the raw edge with nothing behind it.

assembly.title: Fit the ring and trim the gusset
assembly.body: Clip the ring round the back panel and trim the gusset to length — target {gusset_cut}, so that with a {lap} lap at each end onto the zipper panel the ring closes at {ring}. Two strips lapped by {lap} cover their combined length LESS {lap}, so only one of the pair may carry that allowance: the zipper panel does, and the gusset is trimmed to the bare figure. Cut long, fit, then trim — the ring's true length depends on the allowance you actually achieve and on how hard the binding pulls, which is why good patterns give more than the calculation and let you trim.

figures.caption: Trim to the bare figure: only ONE of a lapped pair may carry the allowance, and the zipper panel is the one that does.

assembly.title: Ring anchors onto the gusset interior
assembly.stitch: straight, both long edges, 3.0 mm, walking foot
assembly.body: Each D-ring needs something behind it or the whole bag hangs off two stitch fields in one layer of shell. Lay a {ring_anchor_len} × {ring_anchor_w} strip across the gusset's INSIDE face at each ring position, running the gusset's full cut width so both of its ends finish flush with the panel edges — the panel bindings will catch them, and the load then spreads into a seam that is carrying the bag anyway. Topstitch both long edges. Do it NOW, while the gusset is still a flat strip: it has just been trimmed, so the ring positions are fixed, and once the lap joins are closed you are sewing inside a {ring} loop. Same reason the chassis webbing goes on before the joins. This is the chassis's argument over a shorter span, and it is why a bag can drop the chassis and still take a strap.

figures.caption: Topstitched along both LONG edges — not box-X'd. That tack belongs to the D-ring tab, two steps on.

assembly.title: First lap join
assembly.stitch: straight, two rows, 3.0 mm
assembly.body: Lap one gusset end onto one end of the zipper panel by {lap} and topstitch two rows.

figures.caption: One end only. Leave the other loose — the ring is easier to fit to the panel while it is still a strip.

assembly.title: Close the chassis loop across the top face
assembly.stitch: straight 3.0 mm, then box-X twice round at 2.5–3.0 mm
assembly.body: Lay both webbing tails along the zipper panel's interior centreline; they overlap each other by {overlap} at its centre. Topstitch them down, then box-X both ends of the overlap. The chassis is now one unbroken loop. Doing this before the second lap join is what keeps every webbing pass flat under the foot.

figures.caption: Where the loop closes: across the top face, clear of the coil. The overlap is box-X'd as before.

assembly.title: Second lap join
assembly.stitch: straight, two rows, 3.0 mm
assembly.body: Close the remaining gusset-to-zipper-panel lap, stitching through the webbing where it crosses so the join is reinforced. Both joins land at the top corners, which is also where the binding will mitre — hand-wheel them.

figures.caption: This one closes the loop. Both joins land where the binding will mitre, so hand-wheel them.

assembly.title: D-ring tabs, from the outside
assembly.stitch: box-X, twice round, 2.5–3.0 mm
assembly.body: Fold each 4" tab through its ring and box-X it to the EXTERIOR of the gusset, driving the stitch through tab, gusset and whatever backs it — the internal chassis, or the anchor strip — all at once. The tack is the connection, not the tab. Roughly 1½" × ¾". This is the thickest stack on the bag: hand-wheel every one, and put a height-compensation scrap under the back of the foot so it does not tip.

figures.caption: Where the rings land. The tack goes through tab + gusset + anchor, so it is the thickest stack on the bag.

assembly.title: Grab handle
assembly.stitch: box-X, twice round, 2.5–3.0 mm
assembly.body: Fold 1" under at each end of the {handle} length and box-X both ends to the top face, through to the internal webbing where there is any. Keep both tacks clear of the chassis overlap. Check the handle arcs clear of the slider before committing the second tack — a handle that fouls the zipper is only discoverable at this point and only fixable by unpicking a box-X.

figures.caption: Both ends tacked through the gusset and the webbing behind it.

assembly.title: Divider pocket onto the {divider_face} panel's interior
assembly.stitch: binding at 3.5 mm, channels straight at 3.0 mm
assembly.body:
Finish the {divider_w} × {divider_h} divider's TOP edge — a shell that melt-seals needs only a pass with a knife or a lighter, one that ravels needs binding or a hem. It is the pocket's mouth and the only edge that gets any treatment of its own. Lay it on the panel's interior {divider_inset} clear of the panel's edges on the left, right and bottom, and topstitch those three sides down. Then topstitch the channel lines from the divider side, straight down through divider and panel. The pocket finishes {divider_depth} deep with {divider_clear} of open panel above it to reach past.

**Prefer the bound divider where the shell allows it.** Keeping this one out of the binding costs three straight topstitch runs to save one bound edge, and it puts the pocket's bottom seam in the middle of a panel rather than on a seam that was structural already. It earns its place when the binding is already at the machine's limit, or when the divider is genuinely smaller than the panel it sits on.

figures.caption: Topstitched: three straight runs of its own, inset clear of the binding.

assembly.title: Divider pocket into the {divider_face} panel's binding
assembly.stitch: binding at 3.5 mm, channels straight at 3.0 mm
assembly.body: Bind the {divider_w} × {divider_h} divider's TOP edge first and leave it free — it is the pocket's mouth and the only edge of it that gets a seam of its own. Then lay it on the INTERIOR of the {divider_face} panel with its sides and bottom flush to the panel's raw edges and clip: that panel's own binding catches all three, so the pocket's contents rest on a seam that was structural already rather than on a stitch line invented in the middle of a panel. Topstitch the channel lines from the divider side, through divider and panel. The pocket finishes {divider_depth} deep with {divider_clear} of open panel above it. Three layers now meet in that panel's bound seam, and the binding strip is sized from it.

figures.caption: Bound: cut to the panel's own size, so its sides and bottom are caught in a seam that was being sewn anyway. Only its top edge is a new seam.

assembly.title: Pocketed panel, zip ACROSS — two layers, pocket between them
assembly.stitch: straight, two rows, 3.0 mm, zipper foot, Microtex 90/14
assembly.body:
A panel that carries a pocket is not one piece and it is not two. The OUTER layer is the one the zip is cut into: lap the {top_upper} upper and the {top_lower} lower onto the pocket zipper's tape by {lap} each and topstitch two rows, exactly as you did the gusset's zipper panel. The reassembled outer measures {panel_h}, matching the inner, and both pieces are {panel_w} wide. The INNER layer is a full {panel_w} × {panel_h} panel — the compartment's wall, bound on all four edges like any panel, and the reason the pocket is a sealed space rather than a second way into the bag. Lay outer over inner, wrong sides together, and from here treat the pair as one panel: the pocket is the cavity between them and the zip is its only mouth. Shorten the zipper and bar-tack a new stop just inside the seam line at both ends — the ends themselves get bound over.

The zip sits {top_zip} down from the cut edge and {top_reach} of cavity hangs below it. That band above it is the only material anything tacked to this panel can live in — see the keeper step.

figures.caption: In section: the inner layer is the compartment wall, and the pocket is the cavity in front of it.

assembly.title: Pocketed panel, zip DOWN — two layers, pocket between them
assembly.stitch: straight, two rows, 3.0 mm, zipper foot, Microtex 90/14
assembly.body:
Same sandwich, turned. The OUTER layer splits into a NEAR piece {side_near} wide and a FAR piece {side_far} wide, both {side_across} tall, lapped onto the zipper tape by {lap} each and topstitched two rows. The reassembled outer measures {panel_w}. The INNER layer is a full {panel_w} × {panel_h} panel — the compartment's wall, bound on all four edges like any panel, and the reason the pocket is a sealed space rather than a second way into the bag. Lay outer over inner, wrong sides together, and from here treat the pair as one panel: the pocket is the cavity between them and the zip is its only mouth. Shorten the zipper and bar-tack a new stop just inside the seam line at both ends — the ends themselves get bound over.

**Turning the zip changes two things beyond how obvious it is.** Neither outer piece hangs from the coil when it is open — each is still caught in the binding along its own outer edge, where a horizontal split leaves the lower piece hanging from the zipper alone. And the keepers stop competing with the pocket for the same panel: they sit on the far piece instead of in a band above the zip, so belt width and pocket depth are no longer the same {side_across}. The cavity reaches {side_reach} beyond the opening.

The zip is {side_zip} in from the panel's cut edge, and it does not have to run the whole way: here it starts {side_starts} down from the top and runs {side_run}. Above that stop the two outer pieces lap onto EACH OTHER instead of onto tape — same lap, same two rows, one continuous seam line — so only the zipper is short. Bar-tack a stop at the top of the run. Both outer pieces reach the panel's bottom edge, so BOTH are cut round the corner template — not just one, as when the zip runs across.

figures.caption: On the panel: the run is vertical and stops short of the top, which is what frees the band the keepers need.

assembly.title: Placket over the pocket zip
assembly.stitch: caught in the lap's two rows, 3.0 mm, zipper foot
assembly.body:
The flap that hides the zip. Lay the {side_placket_long} × {side_placket} placket over the NEAR piece with its edge level, so {lap} of it is caught in the two rows that lap that piece onto the tape and {side_placket_show} hangs free across the coil. It is caught in a seam you are already sewing: no new seam, one more cut piece, and one more layer in that lap — panel + placket + tape.

Its free edge is left RAW. The shell does not ravel, and a hem there would double the one thing the placket has to stay: limp enough to lie flat over a coil. Do not press it — a coated shell will not take heat.

It earns its place twice. It keeps the opening from reading as a line across the panel, which is the whole point on the face that goes against the body. And on a waterproof shell it is a rain cover over the most perforated line on the bag: two rows of topstitching through zipper tape, in a coating that does not close behind a needle.

figures.caption: The flap, over the coil, on the face that goes against the body.

assembly.title: Belt keepers, through both layers of the back panel
assembly.stitch: box-X, twice round, 2.5–3.0 mm
assembly.body: The back pocket has already given this panel two layers, and the inner one is bound on all four edges — a better keeper anchor than any strip, so there is no anchor strip to cut. Fold each {keeper_w} × {keeper_len} keeper around a scrap of the belt itself to get the tunnel right, then box-X both ends through keeper, outer panel AND inner panel at once. That is what keeps the bag whole with the pocket zip open under load: the belt pulls on a panel bound to the gusset ring on every side, and the zip is nowhere in the load path. Both tacks sit above the zip, so neither crosses the pocket. Do it before the panel goes into the ring.

figures.caption: Both tacks sit above the zip, so neither crosses the pocket.
Why above: there the box-X reaches the inner layer, which is bound on four sides. Below the zip the only attachment upward is the zipper.

assembly.title: Belt keepers, and the anchor behind them
assembly.stitch: box-X, twice round, 2.5–3.0 mm
assembly.body: Lay the {panel_w} anchor strip on the INTERIOR of the back panel behind where the keepers will sit, with its ends flush to the panel's side edges — the binding will catch them, so the belt load spreads into a seam that is carrying the bag anyway rather than terminating in a stitch field. Then fold each {keeper_w} × {keeper_len} keeper around a scrap of the belt itself to get the tunnel right, and box-X both ends through keeper, panel and anchor at once. Do all of it BEFORE the panel goes into the gusset ring, so the binding catches nothing but the panel edge. Size it to the belt you own: a keeper cut for a 1½" belt will not go over a 2" one, and one cut for 2" flaps on a 1½".

assembly.title: Belt keeper onto the back panel
assembly.stitch: box-X, twice round, 2.5–3.0 mm
assembly.body: Fold the {keeper_w} × {keeper_len} keeper and box-X both ends to the back panel BEFORE it goes into the gusset ring, so the binding catches nothing but the panel edge. Size it to the belt you own: a keeper cut for a 1½" belt will not go over a 2" one, and one cut for 2" flaps on a 1½".

assembly.title: Build the back panel — applied pockets and ribs
assembly.stitch: straight, 3.5 mm, walking foot
assembly.body: Bind any pocket's top edge, then lay the pocket on the panel's interior with its bottom and side edges flush to the panel edges and clip. A full-width pocket has no bottom seam of its own — its contents rest on the panel's own binding, which is structural already, instead of on a loaded stitch line in the middle of the panel. Lay any rib on the exterior and topstitch both long edges: those two lines go through rib, panel and pocket at once and make the divider.

assembly.title: Back panel on, and bound
assembly.stitch: straight, 3.5 mm, {sa} from the panels' raw edges
assembly.body:
Clip the gusset ring around the back panel, raw edges out, matching the gusset seams to the top corners. The gusset's allowance has to splay wherever the outline turns, and it splays two different ways. At each SQUARE corner cut ONE clip to the stitch line. Round each CURVE it has to splay continuously — a flat strip's raw edge must reach a quarter further than its own stitch line there — so relieve it with shallow snips a seam allowance apart, not one deep cut. Then bind the full perimeter in one line, mitring each square corner and easing the bias round each curve. **Sew at {sa} from the RAW EDGES, not at a distance from the binding's own edge.** Every figure in this pattern is measured from the stitch line, and the binding laps over it: it shows {show} on the face while the stitch line is {flange} in from the finished edge, so its inner edge sits {turn} PAST the stitching. Guiding on that edge at ⅛" — which this step used to say — lands the needle at 5/16", and a run that drifts to 5/16" is exactly the failure step 1 tells you to measure for: the ring comes out short of the panels it has to wrap. Set an edge guide off the raw edge.

Set the underside of the binding {turn} deeper than the top: you cannot see the back while you sew, and without that offset a line that looks perfect on top wanders off the binding underneath. Put every binding join mid-edge — never at a corner and never in a curve.

figures.caption: The seam you are about to sew, in section — and why the panel is cut smaller than the bag it makes.
At each square corner. Sew to the intersection and STOP.

assembly.title: Front panel — open the zipper FIRST
assembly.stitch: straight, 3.5 mm, {sa} from the panels' raw edges
assembly.body: Same again, clipping the corners the same way. With the zipper closed you will not get the bag open afterwards, and a bound seam cannot be unpicked — the holes stay. This is the last chance to check the interior is finished.

figures.caption: THE zipper — the main one, on the top face. Open it before this seam, not after.
Set the binding deeper underneath: a line placed by eye on the top face falls off the edge of the binding below it.

assembly.title: Straps, belt and hardware
assembly.body: Webbing through the tri-glides and hooks; box-X each fold, twice round. Everything that clips off is made now, off the bag, where it is flat under the foot. A shoulder pad costs nothing structurally and interface-pressure research is unambiguous that a wider strap is markedly more comfortable.

assembly.title: Thread your belt, clip your strap
assembly.body: Nothing left to sew. The belt is yours: slide it through both keepers and check it runs without binding — if the tunnel is tight, unpick ONE tack, refit the keeper round the actual belt and re-tack, then trim. The strap is yours too and clips to the two D-rings with its own hooks. Unclip it and the bag is a belt bag again; both stay rigged at once.

figures.caption: Nothing left to sew. Check the belt runs without binding before you call it finished.

assembly.title: Base stiffener, loose
assembly.body: Cut it to the INTERIOR, {face_w} × {face_d}, not the exterior, and drop it in. Not sewn — it should come out when the bag is washed.

stitch_schedule.stitch: straight, {sa} from the panels' raw edges

tools.why: Every seam here is a multi-layer sandwich and the layers creep apart under a standard foot. Mandatory if a coated fabric is anywhere in the stack — it sticks to a metal foot and stalls while the feed dogs keep pulling.
For the two rows onto the zipper tape. Not optional; a standard foot cannot get close enough to the coil.

tools.tool: Edge guide, or tape on the throat plate at ⅛"
tools.why: A binding line sewn by eye wanders, and a wandering binding line is the single thing that makes bag work look homemade.
A folded offcut under the back of the foot, to step onto the thickest tacks level. Without it the foot tips and the first stitches bunch.
Never stretch the strip while clipping — stretched binding ripples once the tension comes off. Clips everywhere pins would leave a permanent hole.
The answer to "you cannot pin this". Holds panels, pockets and zip laps exactly in place while you sew. It makes the needle sticky: wipe with alcohol or push it through a bar of soap.

tools.tool: Rotary cutter and a METAL straightedge
tools.why: Coated and natural fabrics do not melt-seal, so they are rotary-cut. A plastic ruler melts against a hot knife.

Webbing and synthetic binding tape only. Check its duty cycle — a 60" strip is 30–45 seconds of unbroken cutting and non-air-cooled units are rated for ~15-second intervals; pausing mid-cut leaves a blob and a restart notch on a strip whose whole job is to be an even width.

checklist.item: A test bound seam sewn on scrap, and the achieved seam allowance measured
The worst stack in the thickness table test-sewn
checklist.why: Changing the tab material is free before cutting and expensive after.
It shrinks and the bag has no ease to absorb it.

checklist.item: Binding is NOT the shell material
checklist.why: A fraying binding must be double-fold: four layers at every seam instead of two, and the mitred corner stops being drivable.

checklist.item: Gusset cut long at {gusset_cut_long} and left long until the ring is fitted
checklist.why: The ring's true length depends on the allowance you achieve.

checklist.item: Gusset ring measures {ring} before the first panel goes on
checklist.why: A ring cut to the raw-edge perimeter is 8 × the seam allowance too long, and that is pucker eased into a seam that cannot take it.

checklist.item: Any panel embroidered before the webbing or pockets go in
checklist.why: It will not hoop flat afterwards.

checklist.item: Coil sits {coil_c} from the zipper panel's cut edge, clear of the centreline
checklist.why: That clearance is what lets the webbing run dead straight.

checklist.item: Chassis overlap box-X'd at both ends
checklist.why: Until both are tacked it is two straps, not one loop.

checklist.item: New zipper stop bar-tacked BEFORE trimming
checklist.why: Trim first and the slider comes off.

checklist.item: Gusset corners clipped to the stitch line before binding
checklist.why: A rectangular gusset cannot turn a square corner unless you clip it.

checklist.item: Zipper open before the front panel seam
checklist.why: Closed, you will never get the bag open, and a bound seam cannot be unpicked.
